rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal-record screening limits)
rules.requirement:
Housing providers may not put criminal-record questions on an application, or ask about criminal records orally or in writing, before making a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises, and lifetime sex-offender registration.

At no point may a provider evaluate any of these records:
- arrests or charges without a conviction
- expunged, pardoned, vacated or otherwise nullified convictions
- juvenile adjudications
- sealed records

After a conditional offer, a provider may consider only:
- convictions for listed serious crimes, or crimes resulting in lifetime registration
- first-degree indictable offenses within 6 years
- second- and third-degree indictable offenses within 4 years
- fourth-degree indictable offenses within 1 year

Withdrawing an offer requires an individualized assessment and a preponderance-of-evidence finding that withdrawal serves a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest. The provider must give written notice stating the reasons with specificity, plus an opportunity to appeal. The applicant may request the relied-upon information within 30 days, and the provider must supply it free within 10 days.

Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed, and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracies or rehabilitation. Providers may not require drug or alcohol tests or consent to obtain drug-treatment records. They may not publish advertisements excluding applicants with records.

Enforcement is only through complaints to the Division on Civil Rights, with no court actions, and a 14-day mediation window. Penalties are up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations. The director may also order return of the application fee.
rules.key_value: Post-offer lookback: 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); no lookback for listed serious crimes or lifetime registration. Records request within 30 days, provider response within 10 days. Penalties up to $1,000 / $5,000 / $10,000.

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap ($50, CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement:
A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes.

Starting January 1 of the year after enactment, the cap is adjusted annually in proportion to the CPI-U for New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island. An adjustment is made only if the percent change is greater than zero. The Director of Consumer Affairs publishes the cap each year.

Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each subsequent offense, enforced in Special Civil Part summary proceedings. The amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant. The Director must adopt rules, including a mechanism for reporting violations.
rules.key_value: $50 maximum application fee (CPI-adjusted annually from January 1, 2027); penalties up to $500 / $750 / $1,000

rules.exemptions: Dwelling units in one-family or two-family dwellings; Real Estate Commission licensees unless the licensee is the landlord.

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement:
Deposit limits:
- A landlord may collect a security deposit of at most 1.5 times one month's rent.
- Pet deposits and prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, count toward the cap.
- At lease inception, the landlord may require at most the 1.5-month deposit plus the first month's rent.
- Yearly increases may not exceed 10% of the current deposit.

Holding the deposit:
- The deposit remains the tenant's property and must be held in trust, not commingled.
- It must be kept in an interest-bearing account at an insured New Jersey institution. Landlords with 10 or more units may instead use an insured New Jersey money market fund.
- Interest belongs to the tenant.
- Within 30 days of receipt, and at each annual interest payment, the landlord must give written notice of the institution, amount, account type and interest rate.
- If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may have the deposit plus 7% annual interest applied to rent.

Return of the deposit:
- Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions sent by personal delivery or registered or certified mail.
- Return is due within 5 business days if the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation.
- Return is due within 15 business days if the tenant ends the lease under the Safe Housing Act.
- A tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus costs and attorney's fees.
rules.key_value: Max 1.5x one month's rent (2.5x including first month's rent at inception); annual increase max 10%; return within 30 days with itemized deductions (5 business days if displaced, 15 business days on Safe Housing Act termination); double damages for wrongful withholding

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Landlords holding deposits for fewer than 10 units must use an interest-bearing account at an insured New Jersey bank or savings and loan. Landlords with 10 or more units may alternatively use an insured New Jersey-based money market fund.
coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rentals, including mobile homes. Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings are exempt unless the tenant requests compliance in writing.
coverage.owner_conditions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt. The tenant may make the law applicable 30 days after a written request to the landlord.
coverage.other_conditions: The interest-bearing account provisions do not apply to seasonal rentals of not more than 125 consecutive days.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, unless the tenant requests coverage in writing. Seasonal rentals are exempt from the account and interest provisions.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement:
A residential landlord may not evict a tenant or fail to renew a lease, written or oral, without good cause.

The statutory causes are:
- nonpayment of rent
- disorderly conduct
- intentional or grossly negligent damage
- substantial breach of rules or lease covenants after a Notice to Cease
- failure to pay a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with local ordinances
- health and safety removal or correcting an illegal occupancy
- permanent retirement from residential use
- refusal of reasonable lease changes
- habitual late payment
- condominium or cooperative conversion
- owner or buyer occupancy after conversion, or in buildings of three or fewer units
- end of employment-based tenancy
- certain drug, assault, theft and human-trafficking findings

A written Notice to Quit describing the cause is required for every cause except nonpayment. A Notice to Cease is required for some causes, with no statutory period. Only a court judgment and warrant for removal can remove a tenant; self-help eviction is illegal.

Tenants evicted for illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance of six months' rent. A landlord who does not occupy the unit for 6 months after an owner-occupancy eviction is liable for treble damages. So is a landlord who reuses the property residentially within 5 years after a retirement or demolition eviction, which also carries a civil penalty of up to $10,000.

Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings are subject only to a narrower list of causes. Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the same good cause and notice rules, and must give the County Welfare Board 3 working days' notice. Unregistered landlords cannot evict.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit periods by cause: 3 days (disorderly conduct, damage, end of employment, criminal-offense causes); 1 month (rule or lease breach, rent increase, lease changes, habitual late payment); 2 months (owner or buyer occupancy); 3 months (health and safety); 18 months (retirement from residential use); 3 years (conversion). Relocation assistance for illegal occupancy: 6x monthly rent. Treble damages for misuse after eviction; civil penalty up to $10,000.

unverifiable_exemptions: Unit held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies it
Hotel, motel or guest house rented to a transient or seasonal guest
coverage.summary: Applies to most residential rentals, including single-family homes, mobile homes and parks, apartment buildings, and rooming and boarding houses. Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings are subject only to a narrower list of causes.
coverage.owner_conditions:
In owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings, eviction is allowed only for:
- holdover after lease expiry
- nonpayment
- disorderly conduct
- willful damage
- repeated rule violations
- lease violations where a right of re-entry is reserved

Notice to Quit is 3 months for at-will or year-to-year tenancies, 1 month for month-to-month tenancies, and 3 days for disorderly, destructive or rule-violation causes.
coverage.other_conditions: Hotel and motel guests with no alternate residence who live there continuously are covered. Landlords who are not properly registered cannot evict.

rules.exemptions: Transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest house guests. Units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member. Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings are covered only by a narrower list of causes.
rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date. This is a long-standing statute.

Coverage follows the guide's section on owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings. The unconscionability standard for rent increases (2A:18-61.1(f)) belongs here; it is not a state rent cap. rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections and notices (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement:
Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction.

A buyer of a foreclosed property who wants to occupy it as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit. A tenant whose lease runs longer may not be evicted until the lease expires.

Anyone acquiring a foreclosed property with residential rental units must, within 10 business days after the sale, give tenants a notice in English and Spanish. The notice states that ownership has changed and that tenants need not move. In buildings with more than 10 units, the notice is posted in a prominent location instead.

Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule notice of tenant rights. Any monetary offer to induce a tenant to leave must come with a separate notice and a five-day review period. Pressure tactics are prohibited, including harassment and unconscionable rent increases.
rules.key_value: Tenant notice within 10 business days after sale (English and Spanish); 90-day notice to quit for buyer occupancy; 5-day review period for buyout offers

coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental units in foreclosed properties. Month-to-month tenants and owner-occupied two- and three-family units are not exempt from the 90-day notice requirement. In buildings with more than 10 units, posting replaces individual notices.
coverage.other_conditions: Triggered only when a foreclosed property is sold or transferred.

rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
rules.quoted_span: must provide notices to the tenants in English and Spanish, within 10 business days after the sale
rules.review_note: The guide grounds the 90-day notice to quit in case law (Chase Manhattan Bank v. Josephson) and cites no statute for it. The citation reflects the Foreclosure Fairness Act sections the guide names for the notice and buyout duties.
rules.source_notes: Official DCA Truth in Renting guide (secondary summary of the statutes).

rules.title: Reprisal protections for tenants
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of the lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when the tenant exercises protected civil rights. These rights are:
- enforcing rights under the lease or State or local law
- making a good-faith complaint to a governmental authority, after first notifying the landlord in writing and allowing reasonable time to correct the problem
- organizing or joining a lawful tenant organization
- refusing lease changes made in retaliation

A tenant may sue for damages.

coverage.summary: Applies to all rental properties used for dwelling purposes, including mobile homes, except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings.
coverage.owner_conditions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt.

rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.

A landlord cannot take reprisal action against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of

2A:42-10.10).

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (condominium/cooperative conversion)
rules.requirement:
In a building being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership, qualifying tenants may obtain protected tenancy status and be protected from eviction for up to 40 years. Qualifying tenants are:
- tenants aged 62 or older before the conversion recording date
- permanently disabled tenants
- honorably discharged veterans with a service-connected disability of 60% or more

The tenant must have lived in the building at least one year before the recording date. Family income must be no more than three times the county average per-person income, or $50,000, whichever is greater.

The landlord or converter must notify tenants of their right to apply. Applications are generally due within 60 days.
rules.key_value: Eviction protection for up to 40 years; income limit of 3x county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater; applications generally within 60 days

unverifiable_exemptions: Tenant eligibility: age 62 or older before the recording date, permanent disability, or qualifying disabled-veteran status
coverage.summary: Applies to eligible senior, disabled and disabled-veteran tenants in buildings being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership.
coverage.other_conditions: The tenant must have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date.

rules.title: Bar on rent increases to cover condominium/cooperative conversion costs
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. Increases to cover the cost of new services or amenities remain allowed. The bar applies to all tenants in the building, whether or not they qualify for protected tenancy as senior citizens or disabled persons.
rules.key_value: No rent increase to recover costs resulting solely from conversion

coverage.summary: Applies to all tenants in buildings converted or being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership.

rules.exemptions: Increases to cover the cost of new services or amenities are not barred.
rules.effective_date_note: The guide does not state an effective date.
citation_aliases: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act
rules.quoted_span:
rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the 
conversion (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31).
rules.review_note: This is a narrow, conversion-triggered limit, not a general state rent cap. The guide states that New Jersey has no laws establishing or controlling rents; rent control is municipal. Two other state provisions are not recorded here as rent caps. The unconscionability standard for increases sits with the Anti-Eviction Act record. The 30-year new-construction exemption (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5) belongs in municipal rent control coverage. The quoted span reproduces a spacing typo in the source ('cos ts').

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income and other protected characteristics in rental
rules.requirement:
The Law Against Discrimination prohibits discrimination in the sale or rental of housing on these bases:
- race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry or nationality
- sex, gender identity or expression, or affectional or sexual orientation
- marital, civil union, domestic partnership or familial status
- disability
- source of lawful income, or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment

For example, a landlord cannot deny a Section 8 voucher holder an apartment based solely on that source of income. Discriminatory advertising is prohibited.

A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income, an oversized family, a zoning-violating occupancy or poor credit history.

Complaints may be filed with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, free of charge, or in Superior Court within two years. Penalties run up to $10,000 for a first offense.
rules.key_value: Source-of-income discrimination banned (e.g., Section 8 vouchers); DCR complaint within 180 days or Superior Court within 2 years; penalties up to $10,000 for a first offense

unverifiable_exemptions: Rental of a room or rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied as his or her residence
Preference for persons of the same religion by a religious organization
Single-sex residences and housing for older persons (familial status only)
coverage.summary: Applies to the sale or rental of all property, residential or business, except the listed exemptions.
coverage.owner_conditions: Exempt: rental of a single apartment in a two-family dwelling whose other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence at the time of rental.

rules.exemptions:
The following are exempt:
- one apartment in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling
- rooms in an owner- or occupant-occupied one-family dwelling
- religious-organization preference for persons of the same religion
- single-sex residences and housing for older persons, as to familial status only
rules.effective_date_note: Neither source gives an effective date for the source-of-income provision.
rules.quoted_span:
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses.
rules.review_note: Both sources are official summaries: the DCR brochure is rev. 06.18.15, and the DCA guide is undated. The statutory text (N.J.S.A. 10:5-12) is only linked. The guide's statement that landlords may refuse for insufficient income or poor credit cites federal law.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement:
It is unlawful, and a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, for:
- a rental property owner or its agent to pay for, subscribe to or contract for the services of a coordinator
- a coordinator to facilitate a tacit or express agreement restricting competition among rental property owners, including by performing a coordinating function
- two or more persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination
- an agent or subcontractor of a coordinator to engage in parallel pricing coordination
- any person to perform a coordinating function

A coordinating function is algorithmic or automated rent-setting that uses nonpublic, competitively sensitive information of multiple owners, or common algorithms for two or more owners. Antitrust Act remedies (C.56:9-6 through 9-17) apply. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location online and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact ordinances that conflict with the act.
rules.key_value: Violations are New Jersey Antitrust Act violations; effective the first day of the twelfth month after the July 20, 2026 enactment (July 1, 2027); conflicting municipal ordinances prohibited

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Applies to any rental property owner owning, directly or indirectly, one or more rental residential dwelling units. A controlling-interest holder and the owning entity count as a single owner.
coverage.summary: Covers residential dwelling units in New Jersey: houses, apartments, accessory units and other primary residences. Excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.
coverage.other_conditions:
Not coordinating functions:
- research, statistical or testing uses not used to set rents
- free public rent estimates
- equal-terms brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend rents
- government affordability controls

Not algorithmic devices:
- spreadsheets that operate without AI and require human analysis
- databases that only query unprocessed data

rules.exemptions: Excluded from coordinating function: research, statistical analysis or testing not used in setting rents; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage listing databases; government affordability controls. Not algorithmic devices: non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis, and databases that only query unprocessed data. Excluded from residential dwelling unit: inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.
rules.effective_date_note: Section 9 sets the effective date as the first day of the twelfth month next following enactment. Approved July 20, 2026, so this computes to July 1, 2027. The act is not yet effective on the query date.

effective_date_formula.verbatim: This act shall take effect on the first day of the twelfth month next following the date of enactment.

Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent Act
rules.quoted_span:
It
shall be unlawful and a violation of the “New Jersey Antitrust Act,” P.L.1970,
c.73 (C.56:9-1 et seq.) for:
rules.conflict_note: Possible preemption: Section 6(b) prohibits municipalities from enacting ordinances that conflict with the act. Jersey City (Code § 218-12, Ord. 25-057 as amended by Ord. 25-076) and Hoboken (City Code § 158-2) already have algorithmic rent-fixing bans. Those ordinances predate the act and differ in scope, penalties and private enforcement. Whether they conflict and are preempted once the act takes effect on July 1, 2027 is unresolved.

known_gaps.law: Tenant Protection Act of 1992 (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.40 to -61.59; N.J.A.C. 5:24-3.1 to -3.4)
known_gaps.reason: The DCA guide names it only briefly: it extends protected tenancy in condominium and cooperative conversions to qualified tenants in qualified counties, currently only Hudson County. Its text and eligibility terms are not captured, so no separate record was created.

The guide says this law exempts newly constructed multiple dwellings from local rent control for 30 years after construction. It does not cap rents itself, so it is not a state rent_increase_limits record. It belongs in municipal rent control coverage as a new_construction_exemption (years 30, basis completion of construction). No candidate captured it and its text is not provided.
